quote: 2/ Holzgefäss d. h. Schirm {+erhält ziemlich+} den gleichen Druck, wenn der Wind schief stösst als wenn er grade kommt, während bei der graden Wand die Sinuscurve gilt.
english: 2) A wooden vessel, i.e. a screen, receives roughly the same pressure when the wind strikes obliquely as when it comes straight on, whereas for the straight wall the sine curve holds.
topic: The page ends a remark that mathematical statements are as certain as arithmetic with whole numbers (with reference to Kant), lists two hydrodynamic problems about falling walls and wind pressure on a screen, and begins a note of something to say to Gordan.

triage.modern_statement: This is not a mathematical research question. It is an applied fluid-dynamics observation from the 19th century about how wind loads a plate set at an angle. Let α be the angle between the wind and a surface, and let P(α) be the normal pressure on it, written as a fraction of P(90°), the pressure when the wind hits head-on. Hilbert says that for a flat wall P(α) follows a 'sine curve': the Newtonian sin²α law or a sinα law. He contrasts this with a hollow, vessel-like screen, for which P(α) stays roughly constant as α changes. In modern terms the open item is to explain or calculate how the normal force coefficient C_N(α) depends on the body's shape, flat versus concave, at high Reynolds number. Free-streamline (Kirchhoff) theory and experimental aerodynamics are the frameworks for this.
triage.answered_by: No one specifically picked up Hilbert's note. The topic itself was settled by 19th- and early 20th-century theory and experiment. On the theory side, Kirchhoff (1869) and Rayleigh (1876) developed free-streamline flow around plates. On the empirical side, there were rules for inclined surfaces such as Duchemin's formula, P_n = P·2 sinα/(1+sin²α). Langley's experiments around 1891 and later wind-tunnel aerodynamics showed that Newton's sin² law is badly wrong for flat plates, and that the normal force levels off at large angles. I did not search for anything on concave screens in particular.

evidence.claim: Newton's sine-squared law says the force on a flat plate in a moving fluid is proportional to sin² of the angle of attack. This is the 'sine curve' Hilbert means for the straight wall.
Duchemin's formula is a standard engineering formula for wind pressure on surfaces inclined to the wind. It gives the normal component of the pressure.
By 1891, Chanute's Progress in Flying Machines was surveying several competing empirical formulas for the pressure on an inclined surface relative to a surface at right angles.
Kirchhoff's free-streamline flow past an obstacle (1869) is the classical theory for calculating the pressure on plates and polygonal bodies in separated flow.
The AMS Glossary notes that actual wind pressure depends on the shape of the object, so a simple formula should be used with caution.

triage.why: The note jots down an empirical aerodynamic fact (a hollow screen gets about the same pressure at any wind angle; a flat wall follows a sine law) as a problem to think about. It is not a precise mathematical conjecture. It is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem, and I found no source tying it to later work by Hilbert. The underlying physics, how normal force depends on angle and shape, was handled by Kirchhoff and Rayleigh's free-streamline theory, by empirical formulas such as Duchemin's, and by experimental aerodynamics from Langley onward. Today it is routine engineering knowledge measured as force coefficients, not an open research problem. Confidence is medium for three reasons. First, reading 'Holzgefäss' as a concave screen is my interpretation. Second, the search tool hit its usage limit, so I could not verify sources on concave or cup-shaped screens or on Rayleigh's 1876 paper. Third, the evidence entries come from short search snippets, and I could not check the full texts.
